claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification of cellular mRNAs.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification of cellular mRNAs.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: m6A is recognised by YTH domain-containing proteins, which selectively bind to m6A-decorated RNAs regulating their turnover and translation.
source: m6A is recognised by YTH domain-containing proteins, which selectively bind to m6A-decorated RNAs regulating their turnover and translation.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about YTH domain proteins.

claim: Using an m6A-modified hairpin present in the Kaposi's sarcoma associated herpesvirus (KSHV) ORF50 RNA, seven members from the 'Royal family' were identified as putative m6A readers, including SND1.
source: Using an m6A-modified hairpin present in the Kaposi's sarcoma associated herpesvirus (KSHV) ORF50 RNA, we identified seven members from the 'Royal family' as putative m6A readers, including SND1.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA affinity and mass spectrometry experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RIP-seq and eCLIP analysis characterised the SND1 binding profile transcriptome-wide, revealing SND1 as an m6A reader.
source: RIP-seq and eCLIP analysis characterised the SND1 binding profile transcriptome-wide, revealing SND1 as an m6A reader.
evidence: This is supported by the RIP-seq and eCLIP data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The m6A modification of the ORF50 RNA is critical for SND1 binding.
source: We further demonstrate that the m6A modification of the ORF50 RNA is critical for SND1 binding, which in turn stabilises the ORF50 transcript.
evidence: This is supported by the DAA treatment experiments and mutational analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: SND1 binding stabilises the ORF50 transcript.
source: We further demonstrate that the m6A modification of the ORF50 RNA is critical for SND1 binding, which in turn stabilises the ORF50 transcript.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA stability assays shown in Figure 8b.

claim: SND1 depletion leads to inhibition of KSHV early gene expression.
source: Importantly, SND1 depletion leads to inhibition of KSHV early gene expression showing that SND1 is essential for KSHV lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiments in BCBL1 cells shown in Figure 7.

claim: SND1 is essential for KSHV lytic replication.
source: Importantly, SND1 depletion leads to inhibition of KSHV early gene expression showing that SND1 is essential for KSHV lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiments showing reduced viral replication in Figure 7.

claim: Members of the 'Royal family' have m6A-reading ability.
source: This work demonstrates that members of the 'Royal family' have m6A-reading ability, greatly increasing their epigenetic functions beyond protein methylation.
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA experiments showing direct binding of Royal domain proteins to m6A-modified RNA in Figure 3.

claim: m6A-seq allows immunoprecipitation of fragmented m6A-modified RNAs followed by next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis.
source: Despite the identification of this modification over four decades ago, only recently have major breakthroughs in our understanding of this modification been made due to the development of m6A-seq, which allows immunoprecipitation of fragmented m6A-modified RNAs followed by next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis.
evidence: This describes the established m6A-seq methodology.

claim: m6A-seq led to transcriptome-wide maps of cellular m6A modification.
source: m6A-seq and subsequent enhanced versions of the technique led to transcriptome-wide maps of cellular m6A modification (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: METTL3 is a catalytically active methyl-transferase that catalyses m6A addition onto specific RNA sequences containing the DRm6ACH motif.
source: m6A writers have also been identified, a catalytically active methyl-transferase, METTL3 (Wang et al., 2016), together with adapter components, catalyses m6A addition onto specific RNA sequences containing the DRm6ACH motif, where D = A, G or U; R = A or G; H = A, C or U.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: FTO and ALKBH5 are RNA demethylases that can erase m6A marks.
source: The RNA demethylases FTO (Jia et al., 2011) and ALKBH5 (Zheng et al., 2013) can erase m6A marks offering a dynamic regulation of m6A status in RNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: YTH readers directly bind m6A in target RNAs through an aromatic cage.
source: YTH readers directly bind m6A in target RNAs through an aromatic cage (Liao et al., 2018), directing their targets towards different biological fates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: YTHDF2 recruits the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex and promotes degradation of m6A-containing RNAs.
source: YTHDF2 recruits the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex and promotes degradation of m6A-containing RNAs (Du et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: YTHDF1, YTHDF3 and YTHDC2 stimulate mRNA translation of their targets.
source: while YTHDF1, YTHDF3 and YTHDC2 stimulate mRNA translation of their targets (Wang et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: YTHDC1 regulates mRNA splicing.
source: and YTHDC1 regulates mRNA splicing (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: m6A destabilises the local RNA structure in hairpins allowing recruitment of hnRNPC to U-tracts.
source: Other RNA-binding proteins can read m6A indirectly, in a so-called 'm6A switch' mechanism, in which m6A destabilises the local RNA structure in hairpins allowing recruitment of either hnRNPC to U-tracts (Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: m6A destabilises the local RNA structure in hairpins allowing recruitment of hnRNPG to a purine-rich motif.
source: or hnRNPG to a purine-rich motif (Liu et al., 2017), both readers then regulate alternative splicing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IGF2BP proteins enhance mRNA stability and translation of m6A-containing RNAs.
source: Recently, IGF2BP proteins were reported to enhance mRNA stability and translation of m6A-containing RNAs and proposed to be a novel class of m6A readers (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Multiple viruses have been mapped for m6A transcriptome-wide.
source: Due to recent transcriptome-wide m6A mapping of multiple viruses (Kennedy et al., 2016; Lichinchi et al., 2016a; Tirumuru et al., 2016; Gokhale et al., 2016; Lichinchi et al., 2016b; Courtney et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2018; Hesser et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2018), it is becoming evident that there is an interplay between m6A-decorated viral RNA and cellular m6A machinery, resulting in modulation of viral replication output.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is an interplay between m6A-decorated viral RNA and cellular m6A machinery, resulting in modulation of viral replication output.
source: Due to recent transcriptome-wide m6A mapping of multiple viruses (Kennedy et al., 2016; Lichinchi et al., 2016a; Tirumuru et al., 2016; Gokhale et al., 2016; Lichinchi et al., 2016b; Courtney et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2018; Hesser et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2018), it is becoming evident that there is an interplay between m6A-decorated viral RNA and cellular m6A machinery, resulting in modulation of viral replication output.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on viral m6A.

claim: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is a DNA virus responsible for several Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome-associated aggressive malignancies.
source: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is a DNA virus responsible for several Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome-associated aggressive malignancies (Baquero-Pérez and Whitehouse, 2015; Schumann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: KSHV has a biphasic life cycle, with a latent phase and a productive lytic phase.
source: KSHV has a biphasic life cycle, with a latent phase and a productive lytic phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KSHV biology.

claim: During latency, the KSHV episome is dormant in the nucleus of endothelial progenitor cells and B-lymphocytes with few viral latent genes expressed.
source: During latency, the KSHV episome is dormant in the nucleus of endothelial progenitor cells and B-lymphocytes (Giffin and Damania, 2014), with few viral latent genes expressed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Under various stimuli, the KSHV episome can be reactivated into lytic replication, leading to the ordered expression of more than 80 viral proteins.
source: Under various stimuli, the KSHV episome can be reactivated into lytic replication, leading to the ordered expression of more than 80 viral proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KSHV biology.

claim: The replication and transcription activator (RTA) viral protein, which is encoded from open reading frame 50 (ORF50), is the first lytic protein produced and is essential for the latent-lytic switch.
source: The replication and transcription activator (RTA) viral protein, which is encoded from open reading frame 50 (ORF50), is the first lytic protein produced and is essential for the latent-lytic switch (Guito and Lukac, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A novel m6A peak-calling algorithm was used to accurately decipher the KSHV m6A epitranscriptome.
source: Here we accurately decipher the KSHV m6A epitranscriptome using a novel m6A peak-calling algorithm and characterise m6A readers that specifically interact with KSHV m6A-modified RNA sequences found in ORF50 and ORF37.
evidence: This is supported by the methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eight members from the Tudor domain 'Royal family', including SND1, were specifically enriched in m6A-modified KSHV sequences through RNA affinity.
source: Through the use of RNA affinity, in addition to YTH readers, eight members from the Tudor domain 'Royal family', including SND1 (Staphylococcal nuclease domain-containing protein 1), were specifically enriched in m6A-modified KSHV sequences.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data from RNA affinity experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 'Royal family' is a well-characterised family that reads methylated residues in histones through the use of an aromatic cage.
source: The 'Royal family' is a well-characterised family that reads methylated residues in histones through the use of an aromatic cage (Chen et al., 2011) which is structurally similar to the one found in YTH readers (Luo and Tong, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The aromatic cage in the 'Royal family' is structurally similar to the one found in YTH readers.
source: The 'Royal family' is a well-characterised family that reads methylated residues in histones through the use of an aromatic cage (Chen et al., 2011) which is structurally similar to the one found in YTH readers (Luo and Tong, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Electromobility shift assays (EMSAs) demonstrate the ability of specific Royal domains to selectively bind m6A-modified RNA.
source: Electromobility shift assays (EMSAs) demonstrate the ability of specific Royal domains to selectively bind m6A-modified RNA.
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Royal domain binding to m6A-modified RNA may occur in a RNA secondary structure/sequence-dependent manner.
source: As these domains do not bind all m6A-modified RNA sequences it suggests this binding may occur in a RNA secondary structure/sequence-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective binding patterns observed in the EMSA experiments.

claim: A modified RIP-seq technique was developed that significantly improves the resolution of standard RIP.
source: We further developed a modified RIP-seq technique, which significantly improves the resolution of standard RIP, accompanied by a unique bioinformatic analysis to characterise for the first time the transcriptome-wide binding profile of SND1 to cellular and KSHV mRNAs
evidence: This is supported by the methods description and data presented.

claim: SND1 is a bona fide RNA-binding protein that targets m6A-modified RNAs in KSHV-infected cells.
source: revealing SND1 as a bona fide RNA-binding protein that targets m6A-modified RNAs in KSHV-infected cells, including the extensively m6A-modified ORF50 RNA.
evidence: This is supported by the RIP-seq data showing SND1 binding to m6A-modified RNAs.

claim: SND1 eCLIP analysis using publically available datasets deposited in ENCODE confirmed that SND1 has a binding profile similar to other m6A reader proteins.
source: SND1 eCLIP (enhanced crosslinking immunoprecipitation) analysis using publically available datasets deposited in the ENCyclopedia Of DNA Elements (ENCODE) further confirmed that SND1 has a binding profile similar to other m6A reader proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the eCLIP analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Depletion of SND1 in KSHV-infected cells significantly reduced the stability of unspliced ORF50 RNA.
source: Importantly, depletion of SND1 in KSHV-infected cells significantly reduced the stability of unspliced ORF50 RNA and led to markedly reduced levels of RTA protein together with a global impairment of KSHV lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA stability assays shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Depletion of SND1 led to markedly reduced levels of RTA protein.
source: Importantly, depletion of SND1 in KSHV-infected cells significantly reduced the stability of unspliced ORF50 RNA and led to markedly reduced levels of RTA protein together with a global impairment of KSHV lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 7.

claim: Depletion of SND1 led to a global impairment of KSHV lytic replication.
source: Importantly, depletion of SND1 in KSHV-infected cells significantly reduced the stability of unspliced ORF50 RNA and led to markedly reduced levels of RTA protein together with a global impairment of KSHV lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data in Figure 7.

claim: m6A-modification in ORF50 RNA regulates SND1 binding to this RNA, particularly to the unspliced form.
source: Furthermore, we show that m6A-modification in ORF50 RNA regulates SND1 binding to this RNA, particularly to the unspliced form.
evidence: This is supported by the DAA treatment experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: m6aViewer implements a novel m6A peak-calling algorithm that identifies high-confidence methylated residues with more precision than previously described approaches.
source: We have previously developed dedicated software (m6aViewer) which implements a novel m6A peak-calling algorithm that identifies high-confidence methylated residues with more precision than previously described approaches (Antanaviciute et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: m6A-seq was performed in TREx BCBL1-Rta cells in latent cells and cells undergoing lytic replication for 8 hr and 20 hr post-induction in two biological replicates.
source: Utilising this software we mapped m6A modifications in the KSHV transcriptome by performing m6A-seq in TREx BCBL1-Rta cells, a BCBL1-based, primary effusion lymphoma B-cell line containing latent KSHV episomes capable of doxycycline-inducible reactivation of lytic replication. We carried out m6A-seq in latent cells and cells undergoing lytic replication for 8 hr and 20 hr post-induction in two biological replicates.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In latent cells, m6A peaks were consistently observed in six viral RNAs, including ORF72 and ORF73.
source: In latent cells, we consistently observed m6A peaks in six viral RNAs, including ORF72 and ORF73.
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data.

claim: At 8 hr post-reactivation, 33 m6A peaks were identified in 21 KSHV ORFs in both biological replicates.
source: At 8 hr post-reactivation, 33 m6A peaks were identified in 21 KSHV ORFs in both biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: At 20 hr post-reactivation, 75 m6A peaks were mapped in 42 KSHV ORFs.
source: At 20 hr post-reactivation, 75 m6A peaks were mapped in 42 KSHV ORFs (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The positions of m6A peaks were highly reproducible across the different time points and replicates.
source: The positions of these m6A peaks were highly reproducible across the different time points and replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 12 viral m6A peaks were validated by two-step quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR).
source: 12 viral m6A peaks were further validated by two-step quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 18,946 m6A peaks were common to both replicates in latent cells.
source: m6A peaks in cellular RNAs were also consistently called, with 18,946 m6A peaks common to both replicates in latent cells and 18,935 and 13,926 m6A peaks in cells reactivated for 8 hr and 20 hr, respectively (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 18,935 m6A peaks were common to both replicates in cells reactivated for 8 hr.
source: m6A peaks in cellular RNAs were also consistently called, with 18,946 m6A peaks common to both replicates in latent cells and 18,935 and 13,926 m6A peaks in cells reactivated for 8 hr and 20 hr, respectively (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 13,926 m6A peaks were common to both replicates in cells reactivated for 20 hr.
source: m6A peaks in cellular RNAs were also consistently called, with 18,946 m6A peaks common to both replicates in latent cells and 18,935 and 13,926 m6A peaks in cells reactivated for 8 hr and 20 hr, respectively (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-seq data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Cellular m6A peaks remained mostly unchanged between latent and 8 hr of lytic replication.
source: Cellular m6A peaks remained mostly unchanged between latent and 8 hr of lytic replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of m6A peak numbers.

claim: Lower detection of m6A peaks at 20 hr post-reactivation was observed in part due to KSHV-mediated host cell shut-off.
source: Lower detection of m6A peaks at 20 hr post-reactivation was observed in part due to KSHV-mediated host cell shut-off (Conrad, 2009) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The majority of uniquely identified m6A peaks at 20 hr post-reactivation were found in RNAs whose expression was increased during lytic replication.
source: However, the majority of uniquely identified m6A peaks at this time point were found in RNAs whose expression was increased during lytic replication (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Cellular m6A peaks were enriched in the coding region (CDS) and 3' untranslated region (UTR) throughout KSHV infection.
source: Cellular m6A peaks were enriched in the coding region (CDS) and 3' untranslated region (UTR) throughout KSHV infection (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: In viral mRNAs, the majority of m6A peaks were located in the CDS.
source: In viral mRNAs, the majority of m6A peaks were located in the CDS (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The DRm6ACH motif was confirmed both in cellular and viral mRNAs.
source: We also confirmed the DRm6ACH motif both in cellular and viral mRNAs (Figure 1f and g, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 1f and g.

claim: Approximately 60% of viral m6A peaks contained the GGm6AC[G/U] motif.
source: Approximately 60% of viral m6A peaks contained the GGm6AC[G/U] motif, a significant over-representation of the motif when compared to the expected DRm6ACH frequency.
evidence: This is supported by the motif analysis of viral m6A peaks.

claim: The GGm6AC[G/U] motif is significantly over-represented in viral m6A peaks when compared to the expected DRm6ACH frequency.
source: Approximately 60% of viral m6A peaks contained the GGm6AC[G/U] motif, a significant over-representation of the motif when compared to the expected DRm6ACH frequency.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of observed vs expected motif frequencies.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that all three m6A baits enriched for YTH readers.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that all three m6A baits enriched for YTH readers (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The methylated ORF50-1 (m6A-ORF50-1) distinctly enriched SND1, a Tudor domain-containing protein.
source: An intriguing observation was that of the three viral baits, exclusively the methylated ORF50-1 (m6A-ORF50-1) distinctly enriched SND1, a Tudor domain-containing protein.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: SND1 was in the top thirteen enriched protein hits in m6A-ORF50-1 bait, together with YTHDF1, YTHDF2 and YTHDF3.
source: SND1 was in the top thirteen enriched protein hits, together with YTHDF1, YTHDF2 and YTHDF3.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: YTHDF1 was greatly enriched in all three methylated baits.
source: Further binding validation of YTHDF1 and SND1 in RNA affinity experiments demonstrated that YTHDF1 was greatly enriched in all three methylated baits while SND1 showed a modest but clear enrichment exclusively in m6A-ORF50-1 bait (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SND1 showed a modest but clear enrichment exclusively in m6A-ORF50-1 bait.
source: Further binding validation of YTHDF1 and SND1 in RNA affinity experiments demonstrated that YTHDF1 was greatly enriched in all three methylated baits while SND1 showed a modest but clear enrichment exclusively in m6A-ORF50-1 bait (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SND1 binds symmetrically dimethylated arginines (sDMA) via its Tudor domain.
source: SND1 binds symmetrically dimethylated arginines (sDMA) via its Tudor domain (Liu et al., 2010), thus it harbours the ability to selectively recognise methyl groups.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: m6A-ORF50-1 bait also prominently pulled down three spliceosomal proteins known to interact with the Tudor domain of SND1: snRNP200, snRNP116 and PRPF8.
source: In addition to SND1, m6A-ORF50-1 bait also prominently pulled down three spliceosomal proteins known to interact with the Tudor domain of SND1, snRNP200, snRNP116 and PRPF8 (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data and citation to published literature.

claim: snRNP200, snRNP116 and PRPF8 were within the top fifteen enriched protein hits in m6A-ORF50-1 bait.
source: These proteins were within the top fifteen enriched protein hits.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Multiple proteins related to RNA processing were enriched in m6A-ORF50-1 bait.
source: Multiple proteins related to RNA processing were also enriched in this bait (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The Tudor domain 'Royal family' comprises five subfamilies: Tudor, plant agenet, chromo, PWWP and MBT.
source: SND1 belongs to the Tudor domain 'Royal family', comprising five subfamilies: Tudor, plant agenet, chromo, PWWP and MBT (Maurer-Stroh et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Members from each subfamily of the 'Royal family' share a structurally related β-barrel that harbours an aromatic cage implicated in binding methylated arginines and lysines.
source: Members from each subfamily share a structurally related β-barrel that harbours an aromatic cage implicated in binding methylated arginines and lysines (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: All three plant agenet members were exclusively bound to m6A-ORF50-1 bait.
source: Strikingly, several Royal members were also enriched in methylated viral baits. All three plant agenet members, which were recently identified as RNA sequence-dependent m6A readers (Edupuganti et al., 2017; Arguello et al., 2017), were exclusively bound to m6A-ORF50-1 bait (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Plant agenet members were recently identified as RNA sequence-dependent m6A readers.
source: All three plant agenet members, which were recently identified as RNA sequence-dependent m6A readers (Edupuganti et al., 2017; Arguello et al., 2017), were exclusively bound to m6A-ORF50-1 bait (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Three PWWP domain-containing proteins were enriched in m6A-ORF50-1 bait.
source: Three PWWP domain-containing proteins were also enriched in m6A-ORF50-1 bait while m6A-ORF37 bait retrieved the chromo protein CBX3 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: m6A-ORF37 bait retrieved the chromo protein CBX3.
source: Three PWWP domain-containing proteins were also enriched in m6A-ORF50-1 bait while m6A-ORF37 bait retrieved the chromo protein CBX3 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Royal domains may be capable of reading methyl-decorations not only in proteins but also in RNA.
source: These results suggest that Royal domains may be capable of reading methyl-decorations not only in proteins but also in RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of Royal family members in m6A-modified RNA baits.

claim: None of the indirect m6A readers, hnRNPA2B1, hnRNPC or hnRNPG, or IGF2BP proteins were enriched in any of the baits.
source: None of the indirect m6A readers, hnRNPA2B1, hnRNPC or hnRNPG, or IGF2BP proteins were enriched in any of the baits (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Eight proteins with methyl-transferase activity were recruited to methylated baits.
source: Eight proteins with methyl-transferase activity were also recruited to methylated baits (Supplementary file 2), of these, METTL16 is the second m6A methyltransferase identified to date (Pendleton et al., 2017), which methylates structured RNAs where the adenosine is present in a bulge in the nonamer sequence UACAGAGAA, where A is modified (Mendel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: METTL16 is the second m6A methyltransferase identified to date.
source: Eight proteins with methyl-transferase activity were also recruited to methylated baits (Supplementary file 2), of these, METTL16 is the second m6A methyltransferase identified to date (Pendleton et al., 2017), which methylates structured RNAs where the adenosine is present in a bulge in the nonamer sequence UACAGAGAA, where A is modified (Mendel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: METTL16 methylates structured RNAs where the adenosine is present in a bulge in the nonamer sequence UACAGAGAA.
source: Eight proteins with methyl-transferase activity were also recruited to methylated baits (Supplementary file 2), of these, METTL16 is the second m6A methyltransferase identified to date (Pendleton et al., 2017), which methylates structured RNAs where the adenosine is present in a bulge in the nonamer sequence UACAGAGAA, where A is modified (Mendel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SND1-C-terminus shifted m6A-ORF50-1 bait in contrast to the control bait.
source: Notably, SND1-C-terminus shifted m6A-ORF50-1 bait in contrast to the control bait (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Neither ORF50-4 nor ORF37 methylated baits were selectively bound by SND1-C-terminus.
source: Neither ORF50-4 nor ORF37 methylated baits were selectively bound by SND1-C-terminus (Figure 3c and d, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: m6A-ORF50-1 bait showed two distinct bands when run on its own without any protein, one lower band which migrated at the same speed of A-ORF50-1 bait and another higher band migrating slower.
source: Curiously, when running m6A-ORF50-1 bait on its own (without any protein), two distinct bands were visualised, one lower band which migrated at the same speed of A-ORF50-1 bait and another higher band migrating slower (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Electrospray ionisation (ESI) of the ORF50-1 baits showed that there were no truncated forms and that the correct molecular weight of a methyl group had been added (15 daltons), demonstrating the purity of the baits.
source: Electrospray ionisation (ESI) of the ORF50-1 baits showed that there were no truncated forms and that the correct molecular weight of a methyl group had been added (15 daltons), demonstrating the purity of the baits (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the ESI data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: m6A addition to ORF50-1 destabilises the hairpin which then migrates slower compared with the non-methylated bait.
source: As m6A can destabilise local RNA structure in hairpins (Liu et al., 2015), it seems plausible that m6A addition to ORF50-1 destabilises the hairpin which then migrates slower compared with the non-methylated bait.
evidence: This is inferred from the EMSA migration pattern and cited literature on m6A effects on RNA structure.

claim: SND1-C-terminus did not shift the cropped version of ORF50-1 bait (cORF50-1).
source: Remarkably, SND1-C-terminus did not shift this bait (Figure 3e), highlighting that structural features of the RNA ligand are critical for SND1-binding and that the beginning of the m6A-ORF50-1 hairpin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, boxed region) may be required for an interaction with SND1.
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Structural features of the RNA ligand are critical for SND1-binding.
source: Remarkably, SND1-C-terminus did not shift this bait (Figure 3e), highlighting that structural features of the RNA ligand are critical for SND1-binding and that the beginning of the m6A-ORF50-1 hairpin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, boxed region) may be required for an interaction with SND1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential binding to different RNA structures.

claim: The beginning of the m6A-ORF50-1 hairpin may be required for an interaction with SND1.

evidence: This is supported by the localised enrichment analysis.

claim: Native ORF50 RNA was significantly more unstable in SND1-depleted TREx BCBL1-Rta cells.

claim: Point mutation in the motif contained in ORF50-1 bait significantly reduced m6A enrichment, confirming that this site is m6A-modified.
source: Next, we set out to determine whether the m6A status of ORF50 RNA regulates SND1 binding. Firstly, single-point mutations were performed in the GGACU motifs present in ORF50 baits to elucidate whether the chosen motifs were m6A-modified in the context of the full length ORF50 RNA. Wild type (WT) FLAG-ORF50 -containing both ORF50 exons and the intron- and mutant plasmids were transfected into HEK-293 cells and m6A enrichment quantified by m6A-IP-qPCR (Figure 8c). In transfected cells, ORF50 RNA was particularly m6A-modified in ORF50-1 and ORF50-4 regions, suggesting cell type differences between TREx BCBL1-Rta and HEK-293 cells. Point mutation in the motif contained in ORF50-1 bait, but not in ORF50-4 bait, significantly reduced m6A enrichment, confirming that this site is m6A-modified.
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-IP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8c.

evidence: This is supported by the m6A-IP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8c.

evidence: This is supported by the RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: DAA effectively reduced m6A enrichment in all m6A-modified regions of ORF50 RNA.

HEK-293 cells were transfected with WT FLAG-ORF50 plasmid and 4 hr after transfection, control 0.25% (v/v) DMSO or 200 µM DAA was incubated for an additional 24 hr. Note that DAA did not result in cytotoxicity at this concentration after 26 hr post-treatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). DAA effectively reduced m6A enrichment in all m6A-modified regions of ORF50 RNA (Figure 8c)
evidence: This is supported by the m6A-IP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8c.
